_purpose: ✒️ Executive Enactment Record — Phase 3: the wave-1 formal actions, curated from primary sources. This file is the single source of truth for the lane's action data: netlify/database/migrations/20260807000000_seed_exec_actions_wave1.sql writes the same rows into the vr_* spine, and Phase 4 will load the same shape into window.EXEC_ACTIONS. scripts/test-exec-seed.mjs asserts the two agree, so the SQL and the client data cannot drift apart.
_shape: Exactly the shape actionsFor() / standingOf() in exec-record.js already read: actionClass, documentId, title, actedAt, term, sourceUrl, sourceLabel, issues[{issueKey, direction, isPrimary, weight, rationale}], status[{status, effectiveAt, authority, sourceLabel, sourceUrl, basis, note}]. Nothing here is a new vocabulary — every actionClass is a key of db/exec-action-types.json#actionClasses, every direction is a key of #issueDirections, every status is a token of db/exec-summary-keys.json#buckets.actions, and every issueKey is in db/issue-keys.json.

_sourcingRules.sourceOfRecord: Per db/exec-action-types.json: congress.gov for signed legislation, federalregister.gov for orders. whitehouse.gov appears nowhere in this file, not even as a secondary link — every action here had a primary citation available, so no secondary was needed.
_sourcingRules.standingCitation: Every status entry carries its own source_url and source_label, and a `basis` naming what kind of document establishes it. An action with no citable standing gets NO status entry rather than an assumed one; exec-record.js routes it to unstatedStanding and discloses it as 'with no confirmed standing on file'.

basisValues.enacted_law_published: The standing is established by the enrolled text as published by GPO — the law exists and nothing in the file repeals it. Claims enactment and publication; claims nothing about litigation.
basisValues.court_ruling: The standing is established by a ruling this pass read in full from the court's own opinion. The strongest basis, and the only one that can support 'blocked', 'partly blocked' or 'struck down'.
basisValues.register_disposition: The standing is established by the Federal Register document record, whose disposition notes are the authoritative register of revocation and supersession BY LATER PRESIDENTIAL ACTION. Deliberately narrower than court_ruling: it says the order stands as published and unrevoked, and says nothing about any challenge to it. Every entry using this basis states that limit in its note.

_whyNoScore: There is no score field anywhere in this file and no count that could become one. See exec-record.js's header: the set of orders a president could have signed is unbounded and self-chosen, so any ratio computed over these five rows would divide by a number we picked.

_verificationPass.method: Every citation below was fetched and read in this pass, not carried over from curated text. Federal Register facts come from the FR API document records (title, signing date, publication date, FR citation, document number, disposition notes). Public Law facts come from GPO's published PLAW packages. Standing facts come from the courts' own opinions, downloaded as PDF and read — the operative 'For the foregoing reasons' disposition, not a summary of it.
_verificationPass.refused: congress.gov returns HTTP 403 to this environment, as it has to every prior voting-record pass (see 20260804000000's header). The congress.gov bill pages below are cited as the source of record because db/exec-action-types.json names them as such and the repo's whole congressional lane already cites them; the FACTS asserted about those two laws were verified against GPO instead, which does answer.

trump.title: Laken Riley Act
trump._citationNote: S. 5, not H.R. 29, is the vehicle that became Public Law 119-1. The two bills shared the name; the House-numbered one never left the Senate calendar. The repo already had this wrong once and repaired it in 20260804000000 — this seed attaches to the corrected identity, and GPO's PLAW-119publ1 enrolled text carries '[S. 5]' on its face.

issues.rationale: Mandates detention and removal proceedings for covered unauthorized immigrants.
Tightens immigration enforcement.
Triggered by arrest for burglary, theft, larceny, shoplifting, assault of a law enforcement officer, or any crime resulting in death or serious bodily injury.
Gives state attorneys general standing to sue the federal government over certain immigration-detention and enforcement decisions.

trump._issuesNote: Not re-authored here. These are the four vr_measure_issues rows S. 5 already carries, read straight across with supportMeaning yea_supports rendered as direction 'advances'. The EER and the 🏛️ lane therefore cannot disagree about what this law does.

status.authority: Passed by Congress and signed by the President
status.sourceLabel: GovInfo — Public Law 119-1, enrolled text as published by GPO
status.note: Enacted and published as Public Law 119-1, approved January 29, 2025. Nothing on file repeals or amends it. This states that the law exists and stands as published; it is not a statement about any challenge to it.

trump.title: To provide for reconciliation pursuant to title II of H. Con. Res. 14
trump._titleNote: The official title, taken from GPO's PLAW-119publ21. The enacted law carries NO act-wide short title: 'One Big Beautiful Bill Act' does not appear as the name of the Act in the enrolled text, only as a section-level short title deep inside it. The app's congressional-lane data calls the measure by the popular name, which is how readers will search for it, so this row keeps the official title and the popular name is left where it already is rather than being propagated into a second lane. Flagged in the Phase 3 notes; not changed here, because renaming a measure the 🏛️ lane renders is not a seed's business.

issues.rationale: Extends and makes permanent the 2017 individual income-tax rates.
Makes the 2017 individual income-tax rates permanent and adds temporary deductions for tips and overtime pay.
Reduces federal spending across several mandatory programs.
Nonpartisan CBO analysis projects the Act adds trillions of dollars to federal deficits over ten years.
Offsets part of its cost with Medicaid and SNAP reductions the CBO estimates leave millions more people uninsured.
Funds border-barrier construction and border enforcement personnel.
Phases out and repeals clean-energy and electric-vehicle tax credits enacted in 2022.
Appropriates tens of billions of dollars for immigration detention and removal operations.
Raises the child tax credit to $2,200 per child and makes it permanent.
Expands onshore and offshore oil, gas, and coal leasing and speeds fossil-fuel permitting.
Adds a large increase in defense and military spending.
Opens additional federal lands and waters to energy leasing.
Restricts graduate and parent student-loan borrowing and repayment options.
Creates a federal tax credit for donations to K-12 private-school scholarship organizations.

trump._issuesNote: THE OMNIBUS SPLIT, and the reason this lane is not a scoreboard. Fourteen issue mappings, four of them 'opposes' — read across from the vr_measure_issues rows H.R. 1 already carries (five from db/vr-issue-seed.json, nine from 20260720000000_hr1_omnibus_component_issues.sql), with supportMeaning yea_supports/yea_opposes rendered as advances/opposes. One signature therefore reports in both directions, exactly as one roll call on H.R. 1 does in the 🏛️ lane. Curating only the headline issue would have let a signed omnibus look like a single clean win.

status.authority: Passed by Congress and signed by the President
status.sourceLabel: GovInfo — Public Law 119-21, enrolled text as published by GPO
status.note: Enacted and published as Public Law 119-21, approved July 4, 2025. Nothing on file repeals it. This states that the law exists and stands as published; it is not a statement about any challenge to it.

trump.title: Unleashing American Energy
trump._dedupeNote: ONE energy action, not two. The app's curated spotlight data carried this order twice for Trump under one headline that also folded in a second, separate order — 'Declared a national energy emergency to expand production' described BOTH 'Unleashing American Energy' and 'Declaring a National Energy Emergency' (EO 14156, 90 FR 8433, doc 2025-02003, signed the same day). Two documents inside one card cannot be given a standing each, which is precisely what the Standing axis needs. This seed carries EO 14154 alone; EO 14156 is a wave-2 candidate and will arrive as its own row with its own citation and its own standing.

issues.rationale: Directs agencies to expedite oil, gas and mineral permitting and leasing and to remove regulatory barriers to domestic energy production.
Revokes the previous administration's climate executive orders. The Federal Register disposition record for this document lists the revocations by number, including EO 13990 and EO 14008.

trump._issuesNote: The 'opposes' mapping is not an inference about intent — it is read off the Federal Register's own disposition notes for this document, which enumerate the orders it revokes. That is why a sole-authored order can also report in both directions.

status.sourceLabel: Federal Register — Executive Order 14154 document record, 90 FR 8353
status.note: Published at 90 FR 8353 and not revoked or superseded by any later presidential action in the Federal Register's disposition record for this document. That is the whole of the claim: it describes the order's status in the register, NOT the outcome of any challenge to it. This pass found no ruling enjoining EO 14154 itself; the litigation it appears in concerns agency implementation of funding provisions, and the appellate ruling there (4th Cir. No. 25-1575, decided 2026-01-21) vacated the district court's injunctions rather than extending them.

trump.title: Ending Radical and Wasteful Government DEI Programs and Preferencing

issues.rationale: Directs the termination of federal diversity, equity and inclusion offices, positions, programs and related grants and contracts.

status.authority: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
status.sourceLabel: Fourth Circuit — National Association of Diversity Officers in Higher Education v. Trump, No. 25-1189 (published opinion, Feb. 6, 2026)
status.note: The facial challenge to this order reached judgment: the Fourth Circuit VACATED the district court's preliminary injunction and remanded for further proceedings, so no injunction against the order is in effect. Read from the court's own published opinion, which closes 'we vacate the district court's order granting plaintiffs' motion for a preliminary injunction, and remand for further proceedings. VACATED AND REMANDED'. The case continues on remand; a later ruling would arrive as a further row in this log rather than a change to this one.

trump._standingBackfill: The earlier history is real and is NOT yet on file: the district court had preliminarily enjoined parts of this order in February 2025 and the Fourth Circuit stayed that injunction in March 2025. Both belong in this append-only log, and both are held back for the same reason everything else in this lane is held back — this pass did not read either document from a primary source, and a status row cannot cite an opinion it has not opened. Wave-2 backfill, additive, no rewrite: the log is append-only precisely so the history can be filled in behind the current standing.

trump.title: Preserving and Protecting the Integrity of American Elections

issues.rationale: Section 2(a) directs the Election Assistance Commission to require documentary proof of United States citizenship on the federal voter-registration form.
Directs federal agencies to share data to identify ineligible registrants and directs enforcement of ballot-receipt deadlines against States that count late-arriving ballots.

trump._axisBNote: THE WORKED EXAMPLE FOR THE WHOLE LANE, and the reason the standing log is append-only. Three rulings, three citations, one row each — a mutable status column would have kept only the last and lost the other two. Every entry stays 'partly blocked': parts of this order are permanently enjoined and other parts are not, and neither 'in force' nor 'blocked' would be a true one-word answer at any point in this sequence.

status.sourceLabel: D.D.C. — LULAC v. Executive Office of the President, Nos. 25-0946 / 25-0952 / 25-0955 (CKK), Memorandum Opinion of Apr. 24, 2025
status.note: Sections 2(a) and 2(d) PRELIMINARILY ENJOINED; the motions were DENIED as to Sections 2(b), 7(a) and 7(b), which were left free to operate. Read from the court's own opinion, whose disposition names each section separately.

status.authority: U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia (Judge Colleen Kollar-Kotelly)
status.sourceLabel: D.D.C. — LULAC v. Executive Office of the President, Nos. 25-0946 / 25-0952 / 25-0955 (CKK), Memorandum Opinion of Oct. 31, 2025
status.note: Escalation, not resolution: on partial summary judgment the court PERMANENTLY ENJOINED implementation of Section 2(a) and entered a final, appealable judgment on those separation-of-powers claims. Certain Administrative Procedure Act claims were dismissed without prejudice for want of final agency action. The rest of the order was not enjoined, so the standing stays 'partly blocked'.

status.authority: U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia (Judge Colleen Kollar-Kotelly)
status.sourceLabel: D.D.C. — LULAC v. Executive Office of the President, Nos. 25-0946 / 25-0952 / 25-0955 (CKK), Memorandum Opinion of Jan. 30, 2026
status.note: The current standing. The court DECLARED that Sections 2(d) and 3(d) cannot lawfully be implemented and PERMANENTLY ENJOINED them; dismissed the claims directed at Sections 4(a), 7(a) and 7(b) for want of standing or final agency action; and left claims touching Sections 2(b) and 3(a) for further proceedings, subject to strict Privacy Act compliance. Parts of the order are permanently enjoined and parts are still operative — which is what 'partly blocked' means, and why one word for the whole order would be false either way.
